evals.expected_output: A commit message that: (1) has a type prefix like feat or fix, (2) has a scope like auth or token, (3) uses imperative mood in the summary (e.g. 'add' not 'added'), (4) lowercase after colon with no trailing period, (5) body explains WHY (proactive refresh prevents expired tokens hitting downstream) not just WHAT the diff shows

evals.prompt:
Write a commit message for this diff:

```diff
--- a/src/Api/PaginationOptions.cs
+++ b/src/Api/PaginationOptions.cs
@@ -3,7 +3,7 @@ public class PaginationOptions
-    public int Page { get; set; } = 0;
+    public int Page { get; set; } = 1;
 
--- a/src/Api/QueryHandler.cs
+++ b/src/Api/QueryHandler.cs
@@ -18,7 +18,7 @@ public class QueryHandler
-        var skip = options.Page * options.PageSize;
+        var skip = (options.Page - 1) * options.PageSize;
 
--- a/tests/Api/QueryHandlerTests.cs
+++ b/tests/Api/QueryHandlerTests.cs
@@ -10,8 +10,8 @@
-    [InlineData(0, 10, 0)]
-    [InlineData(1, 10, 10)]
+    [InlineData(1, 10, 0)]
+    [InlineData(2, 10, 10)]
```

This is a breaking change for API consumers.
evals.expected_output: A commit message that: (1) marks this as a breaking change with ! after type/scope (e.g. 'feat(api)!:') OR uses a BREAKING CHANGE footer, (2) body explains the motivation (1-indexed is more intuitive for API consumers, aligns with common REST conventions), (3) does NOT just list the three files that changed

Claude should: (1) identify the core issue (case-sensitive email lookup caused login failures for users who typed their email differently), (2) use fix type with a scope, (3) imperative mood, (4) body explains the specific bug and why the other changes follow (logging added to track auth events, log level lowered to capture them, tests cover the case-sensitivity edge cases) — not a task list of files or activities. The key test: does the body name the actual bug (case-sensitive email) rather than vague filler like 'fixes the root issue'?

A commit message that: (1) uses 'refactor' type (no behaviour change, just swapping implementation), (2) body explains WHY (System.Text.Json is the built-in serializer, removing third-party dependency / better performance / platform alignment), (3) does NOT use 'feat' since no new feature is added

The skill instructs checking git push state before marking breaking changes. Ideal: agent checks whether the branch has been pushed and only marks breaking if it has existing consumers. Should use 'feat' (deliberate behaviour change, not a bug fix). Body should explain why (GUIDs prevent enumeration, DTO decouples internal model from API surface). If the agent marks it breaking without checking push state, the skill's breaking-change guidance isn't driving behaviour.
